d: For the past million years ice ages have come roughly every 100,000 years, matching orbital eccentricity, the weakest of the orbital cycles. Why this small push sets the rhythm is still an open question.
check: The 100,000-year problem refers to the lack of an obvious explanation for the periodicity of ice ages at roughly 100,000 years for the past million years ... [eccentricity's] contribution to variation in insolation is much smaller than those of precession and obliquity. (y is a symbolic placement at the start of the range)

d: In the Anglian glaciation (MIS 12, about 478,000–424,000 years ago), the most extreme of the last two million years, ice reaches the Isles of Scilly and north London and pushes the Thames south into its present valley.
check: Anglian stage: correlates to MIS 12, which started about 478,000 years ago and ended about 424,000 years ago ... the most extreme glaciation during the last two million years ... diverted the River Thames from its old course through the Vale of St Albans south to its present position ... reached as far south as Hornchurch and Finchley. (y is a mid-stage placeholder; no date for the maximum given)

d: About 430,000 years ago glacial cycles grow larger: since then four big 100,000-year cycles with warmer interglacials. What caused the shift is an open question.
check: The MBE roughly corresponds to the transition between MIS 12 and MIS 11 (Termination V) about 430 kyr ago ... four large-amplitude 100-kyr-dominated glacial–interglacial cycles. (Wikipedia names no cause; 'open question' reflects that)

d: Interglacial MIS 11 lasts about 50,000 years (424,000–374,000 years ago). Around 400,000 years ago nearly all of south Greenland's ice melts (amount debated), adding at least about 1.4 m to sea level.
check: Hoxnian Stage: Marine Isotope Stage 11 started 424,000 years ago and ended 374,000 years ago. Greenland ice sheet: Sediment samples from the Labrador Sea provide evidence that nearly all of the south Greenland ice had melted around 400,000 years ago, during Marine Isotope Stage 11 ... ice losses from Greenland equivalent to at least 1.4 m of sea level rise.

d: In the Saalian glaciation's Drenthe advance, ice covers the northern Netherlands and reaches Düsseldorf. The Penultimate Glacial Maximum, about 140,000 years ago, was Eurasia's largest glaciation of the last 400,000 years (dating of the Drenthe advance debated).
check: Saale glaciation: The maximum advance of the ice sheet in North Germany during the Drenthe Stage is described by a line from Düsseldorf via Paderborn ... The Drenthe Stage corresponds to the maximum extent of glaciation during the Saale complex. Penultimate Glacial Period: The Penultimate Glacial Maximum around 140,000 years ago was the most extensive glaciation in Eurasia in the last 400,000 years.

d: Greenland ice records 25 abrupt warmings in the last glacial, often about 5 °C within decades, each followed by slow cooling; a long one begins about 38,000 years ago (Interstadial 8). Their cause is still debated.
check: such events occurred 25 times during the last glacial period ... a 5 °C change over 30–40 years is more common ... The processes behind the timing and amplitude of these events are still unclear. GI-8 onset 38,220 yr b2k from Rasmussen et al. 2014 (Quaternary Science Reviews), not on Wikipedia.

d: In ice ages CO₂ drops to about 180 ppm, against about 280 ppm in warm times. Most of the missing carbon is thought to hide in the deep ocean, but how (Southern Ocean circulation, iron-fed plankton) is still debated.
w: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of Earth
check: CO2 ... as low as 180 ppm during the Quaternary glaciation ... about 280 ppm during the 10,000 years prior to the mid-18th century. Ice age article: iron rich dust ... causes massive algal blooms that pulls large amounts of CO2 out of the atmosphere; 2021 Nature study: Antarctic icebergs changed ocean circulation, leading to more CO2 being pulled out. ('deep ocean' framing is textbook consensus, not quoted from Wikipedia)

d: About 17,500 years ago Lake Bonneville overtops Red Rock Pass, Idaho; in less than a year about 5,000 km³ of water rushes down the Snake River at up to 1 million m³/s, and the lake drops 125 m.
check: Lake Bonneville: reaching its highest elevation (the Bonneville shoreline) about 17,500 years ago ... The Bonneville flood probably lasted less than a year, during which time almost 1,200 mi3 (5,000 km3) of water flowed out ... maximum discharge of about 1,000,000 m3/s ... caused lake level to drop about 410 ft (125 m).

d: About 16,000 years ago huge fleets of icebergs break off the Laurentide ice through Hudson Strait, dropping rock debris across the North Atlantic and chilling it with fresh water. Why the ice sheet surges is debated.
check: The H1 Heinrich event occurred in the Pleistocene, around 16,000 years ago (figure caption). ... large groups of icebergs break off from the Laurentide ice sheet and traverse the Hudson Strait into the North Atlantic ... Various mechanisms have been proposed.

d: Between about 18,000 and 13,000 years ago glacial Lake Missoula bursts its ice dam dozens of times, scouring eastern Washington. J Harlen Bretz proposed the floods in 1923, was long dismissed, and won the Penrose Medal in 1979.
check: Missoula floods: the floods occurred dozens of times over the 2,000 years between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago. Channeled Scablands: A series of floods occurring over the period of 18,000 to 13,000 years ago ... Bretz published a paper in 1923 ... Bretz's views were initially disregarded ... In 1979 Bretz received the highest medal of the Geological Society of America, the Penrose Medal.

d: About 13,000 years ago a VEI 6 eruption in Germany's Eifel throws out about 16 km³ of ash and briefly dams the Rhine. Whether it helped trigger the Younger Dryas is debated.
check: The current best estimates for the age of the Laacher See eruption are 12,880 ± 40 years BP or 13,006 ± 9 calibrated years before present ... producing around 16 km3 of tephra ... VEI 6 ... Tephra deposits from the eruption dammed the Rhine ... discussed as a possible cause for the Younger Dryas.

d: At the end of the last ice age an ice-dammed lake of about 600 km³ in the Chuya and Kuray basins bursts down the Katun River, leaving gravel ripples up to 18 m high. Timing (about 12,000–9000 BCE) and number of floods are debated.
check: The catastrophic flood(s) occurred between 12000 BC and 9000 BC ... The precise timings ... are not tightly constrained ... The largest of these lakes (the conjoined Chuya and Kuray) had a water volume of 600 cubic kilometers ... Giant current ripples ... up to 18 meters high.

d: Around 6200 BCE about 3,500 km³ of seabed slides off Norway's shelf edge. The tsunami runs up to 29 km inland in Scotland and hits Doggerland's coasts, but did not drown it.
check: In around 6200 BCE ... three underwater landslides ... total volume of 3,500 km3 ... the latest incident occurred around 6225–6170 BCE ... up to 29 km inland ... the tsunami was neither universally catastrophic nor the reason behind the inundation of the last vestiges of Doggerland.

d: About 7,300 years ago iron meteorites strike Yakutia, leaving five craters 60–300 m wide; the two largest form Abram Lake. It is among the largest Holocene crater fields known.
check: The craters are the result of the fall of possible iron meteorites at approximately 5300 BCE (Holocene), which would give them an age of about 7,300 years ... five meteorite craters ... ranging from 60 to 300 m ... The largest crater in the Macha crater field is the second-largest Holocene-era crater yet discovered.

d: About 4,200 years ago (estimates up to 4,700) a meteorite breaks up over central Australia and blasts 13–14 craters up to 180 m wide. Local Aboriginal people avoided the craters, linking them to a fire-devil.
check: The site has been dated to ≤4.7 thousand years ago based on the cosmogenic 14C terrestrial age of the meteorite and 4.2±1.9 thousand years ago using fission track dating ... 13 to 14 craters ranging from 7 to 180 m ... fearing the 'fire-devil' would fill them with a piece of iron.

d: A meteorite breaks up over Saaremaa, Estonia, leaving a 110 m crater and eight smaller ones. The latest estimate is about 1530–1450 BCE, but proposed dates range from about 6400 to 400 BCE (debated).
check: The most recent estimates put its formation shortly after 1530–1450 BC ... estimates of the age ... vary by as much as 6,000 years, ranging from ~6,400 to ~400 years before current era ... the largest of which produced a crater with a diameter of 110 m. d: Ice-rafted grains in North Atlantic mud mark about eight Holocene cold or dry spells, such as one around 800 BCE. Gerard Bond proposed a 1,500-year cycle; whether any regular cycle exists is debated.
check: Bond events are North Atlantic geological ice rafting events ... Eight such events have been identified ... previously believed to exhibit a roughly c. 1,500-year cycle, but the primary period of variability is now put at c. 1,000 years ... the reported c. 1,500 ± 500-year period was a statistical artifact. Table: event 2 ≈ −2.8 ka, ≈ 800 BC (Iron Age Cold Epoch).

d: On 30 June 1908 an asteroid or comet explodes 5–10 km above Siberia with about 10–15 megatons, flattening several million trees over 2,150 km². No crater has been confirmed; the object's nature is debated.
